newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FORECAST - Taiwan April joblessness seen inching up.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Taiwan April joblessness seen inching up.

text.p: Local economists expect Taiwan's April jobless rate to have inched up slightly to 2.896 percent, due in part to a farm epidemic and related pork export ban, a Reuters Poll found on Wednesday.
The unemployment rate stood at 2.79 percent in March.
The official April jobless figure was to be issued at 0300 GMT on May 23 by the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics.
The following table shows local institutions' forecasts for April joblessness, in percent:
Institution forecast
Core Pacific Securities 3.0
Grand Cathay Securities 2.9
HSBC James Capel Taiwan 2.8
National Securities 2.98
Nomura Securities 2.8
Average 2.896

Economists said the expected rise from March would partially reflect job losses on Taiwan's hog farms, where a major outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease detected in late March forced a ban on all pork exports -- a US$1.56 billion a year industry.
"The epidemic will worsen the jobless situation, reversing what had been an improving jobless trend and pushing the rate close to three percent," said Nomura economist Amy Huang.
Grand Cathay Securities vice-president Terry Chen said damage from the farm crisis was being balanced out by other job-creating factors.
"The actual (farm crisis) impact may not be so serious as originally expected, as it will be offset by a stably recovering economy and a bullish stock market," Chen said.
As of late April, Taiwan's stock index had risen some 25 percent in 1997 alone, though May has seen a modest correction.
Economists initially feared the pork export ban could throw as many as 50,000 farmers and meatpackers out of work, adding some 0.5-0.6 percentage points to the island's jobless rate.
Estimates have fallen to less than half of expectations.
"I'd say job losses due to the hog disease likely would be about 20,000," said National Securities economist Lin Kuo-yang.
Joblessness held close to 1.5 percent in 1991-1994 but hit 1.79 percent in 1995 and pushed past three percent in August, September and October 1996 -- an alarming level for Taiwan.
The jobless rate averaged 2.60 percent for all of 1996.

Officials have attributed the shift to higher jobless levels to a fundamental change in Taiwan's economy -- a shift toward service industries from the labour-intensive manufacturing that had engendered the island's dramatic economic development.
-- Taipei Newsroom (2-5080815)
